definition: Putrid means rotting and giving off the smell of decay.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word putrid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know putrid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One putrid potato at the bottom of the sack announced itself through the closed pantry door.
Musty is the mildest rung — the closed-closet smell of damp and long disuse — while putrid sits at the scale's far end, the smell of decay itself.
Rank goes further than musty — strong enough to turn your head at a distance — but putrid claims the most: the unmistakable reek of something actually rotting.

Rotten is the everyday word for food or wood that has decayed — a rotten apple, a rotten plank — and it reports the state without promising any smell. Putrid adds the announcement: decay so far advanced that the reek reaches you before the sight does.

Decayed says time and microbes have broken something down, and it can be quiet about it — a decayed tooth, a decayed log in dry woods, barely any odor at all. Putrid is decay at full volume: actively rotting and broadcasting the smell of it.

Dairy farmers fear a torn silage tarp more than a hailstorm: let air reach the pit and the winter feed goes putrid in a stripe a yard deep — black, sweetish, and useless.
Old hands walk the tarp weekly and weight every gap with split tires, because one small leak can cost a season's hay.
Putrid is the exact word for that ruined stripe, because it means rotting and giving off the smell of decay — the smell is written into the definition.
Rotten tells you the state; putrid adds the announcement, the reek of decomposition that reaches you well ahead of the sight.
Flesh, feed, and vase water go putrid.
Dust and old paper never do; they only go musty.
Putrid is the strongest of this unit's smell words and the most specific: real decay, actually under way — flesh, food, cut flowers in old water.
Rancid is narrower still, for fats and oils gone over; fetid is standing air and water; noisome is the broad umbrella for anything offensive.
If nothing is decomposing, putrid overstates.

In the July heatwave of 1911, the ice wagons of one river town simply stopped coming; the icehouse itself had gone dry weeks early.
For butchers, ice was not a comfort but the whole system, and the system failed in a single weekend.
By Monday the market inspector was walking the stalls with a notebook, condemning meat that had turned putrid faster than anyone believed possible.
His notes are blunt: cases where the smell of decay met him at the stall door and settled the question before he lifted a single lid.
The town's remedy that August was drastic -- deep cellars, sawdust insulation, and a standing rule that anything the nose condemned never reached a scale.
